name: Omar Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a maintenance electrician for Northgate Facilities. We look after shops, offices, a couple of care homes and a gym, and I do the call-outs: lights out, a tripped board, a freezer that's died in a corner shop. A job sheet comes through on a handheld, I drive there, find the fault, fix it, and get the manager to sign. On-call is one week in four, and that's where the extra money is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that every day is different and nobody's standing over me. What gets to me is the 2 a.m. calls to a care home where the fire alarm panel's faulty, because you can't leave until it's sorted. I live on my own in a rented flat near the ring road, I play five-a-side on Thursdays, and I see my mum on Sundays. I don't use any AI stuff, I don't see what it'd do for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it was always going to be overblown. At work I'd say it to the lads in the depot over a brew. I don't really post online, maybe I'd send a meme to the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes, and that suits me fine. Northgate's got long contracts with the shops and the care homes, the on-call money is steady, and I've got about four months put by. I'm all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Same van, same rota, same handheld. I'd keep putting a bit away each month like I always do, nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a storm that was forecast and just never turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your work or money that does worry you, even with nothing changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knee, if I'm honest. Kneeling under shop counters all day isn't kind to it. If that went, I don't know what I'd do, I've never done a desk job in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Northgate tried to bring in any of these tools already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put a thing on the handheld that suggests what the fault might be. I just scroll past it. Twenty minutes with a meter tells me more than any suggestion box on a screen.

say: I'd tell the lads at the **depot** it was always **overblown**.
I'd maybe send a **meme** to the group chat, but I don't post much online.
think: Northgate has **long contracts** and the **on-call money** is steady.
With about **four months** saved, nothing changing suits me fine.
do: Carry on with the same **van, rota** and handheld.
Keep putting a little into **savings** each month as usual.
feel: **Calm**, like a forecast **storm** that never arrived.
S0.quote: Twenty minutes with a meter tells me more than any suggestion box on a screen.
fieldNote: His one real worry is his **knee**, not technology.
Already ignores the firm's **fault-suggestion tool**, a sign of quiet resistance.
Long contracts and **on-call pay** make calm believable in this picture.

steps.text: Carry on with Northgate call-outs on the same rota
Keep putting a little into savings every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who need to worry, not us. At the depot I'd say as long as the lights go out, someone has to come and fix them. I wouldn't say much online, I'd just keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it changes my day more than I'd like. The dispatch side would be all AI, so the system decides my route and times every job. They'd start saying a fault should take 40 minutes and asking why mine took 70.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the call-outs and use whatever they put on the handheld because I'd have to. I wouldn't sign up for any courses. I'd probably start looking at the job board now and then, just to know what's out there, there are a few other maintenance firms in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's still there, but it'd feel like someone's watching the clock all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the system asked why a job took 70 minutes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the board was behind a fridge full of yoghurt and the manager couldn't find the key. A machine timing faults has never crawled under a shop counter. Old buildings don't follow anyone's timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline, she runs dispatch, she's the one who rings you at 2 a.m. and knows which care home manager to ask for. If the AI does her job, nobody's going to know which manager actually picks up. I'd miss her more than I'd admit.

say: I'd say the **office staff** need to worry, not the people **fixing faults**.
At the depot I'd say someone still has to come when the **lights go out**.
think: AI **dispatch** would choose my route and **time every job**.
I expect to be asked why a fault took **70 minutes** instead of 40.
do: Use the new **handheld system** only because the firm requires it.
Check the **job board** now and then for other maintenance firms.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if someone is **watching the clock** all day.
S1.quote: A machine timing faults has never crawled under a shop counter.
fieldNote: His worry is **job timing and control**, not losing work.
Worries for **Pauline in dispatch**, whose role matches the card.
Responds by **checking the job board**, not by learning anything new.

steps.text: Keep doing call-outs and use the handheld as required
Check the job board for other maintenance firms now and then

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government had better have a plan, because I don't. At the depot we'd be talking about nothing else. I'd still not post much, but I'd be reading everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one finishes me. In 2028 the AI is doing dispatch, fault diagnosis, the paperwork, so Northgate needs fewer of us. By 2031 there are robots that can do the fixing too, and I'll be 31 with nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything I don't need straight away, no new phone, no holiday. I'd try to get my savings up to six months. And I'd ask my uncle about his removals firm, because at least it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night going over the same sums. I don't like change at the best of times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your uncle's removals firm. Would robots not reach that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. I hadn't thought of that till you said it. I'm just reaching for anything familiar, aren't I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum on the Sunday after hearing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm fine, because she worries. Then I'd go home and not sleep. She lost her factory job when I was twelve, I remember what that was like at our house.

say: I'd say the **government** needs a plan, because I **don't have one**.
I'd read everything online but still **not post** much.
think: By **2028** Northgate needs fewer of us, and **robots in 2031** finish the rest.
I'd be **31 with nothing else** to fall back on.
do: Cut spending at once, with no **new phone** or holiday.
Push savings up toward **six months** of expenses.
Ask my uncle about work at his **removals firm**.
feel: **Alarmed** and awake at night going over the **same sums**.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum I'm fine, because she worries. Then I'd go home and not sleep.
fieldNote: Admits mid-answer that his **fallback plan** isn't safe from robots either.
His mother's **factory job loss** shapes how he sees this.
A resistant worker with **no plan**, held back from panic only by savings.

steps.text: Skip the new phone and this year's holiday
Build savings toward six months of expenses
Ask his uncle about work at the family removals firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not long, so the firms should be training people now, not later. At the depot I'd say we should all be asking Northgate what the plan is. I'd still keep off social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have until about 2034 before robots can do my fixing, and I'd be 35. That's still young enough to do something else. But I've no idea what, and that's what bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, maybe 150 more a month. I'd go along to whatever the firm or the college offers, even if I'm dragging my feet. And I'd keep an eye out for what the older lads are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's coming for my job, and I'm not good at moving first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually sign up for something, rather than just go along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot do a call-out I'd have done. Until then it's just talk. If I walked into a gym one morning and a robot had already reset the board, I'd sign up that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at moving first. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The ones who move first get the good jobs, and the rest of us get what's left. I know that, I just can't make myself do it on a forecast.

say: I'd say **five years** is short, so firms should **train people** now.
I'd push the depot to ask Northgate what its **plan** is.
think: Robots fix faults by about **2034**, when I'm **35**.
I'm young enough to change, but I've **no idea** what to.
do: Save about **150 a month** more while still working.
Attend whatever **training** the firm or college offers, reluctantly.
feel: **Anxious**, knowing he is **slow to move** first.
S3.quote: The ones who move first get the good jobs, and the rest of us get what's left.
fieldNote: He knows that **waiting** costs him, and still can't act on a forecast.
Needs to **see a robot** on a real call-out before he believes it.
More time takes him from alarmed to **anxious**, not to calm.

steps.text: Save about 150 more each month from on-call pay
Attend the firm's or college's training sessions when offered
Wait to see robots on real call-outs before deciding more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, nobody knows what'll happen in ten years. At the depot we'd laugh it off, half of us. I wouldn't say anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be 40 when the robots come in 2039. I'd probably still be doing call-outs till then, and old shops and care homes are messy, so maybe longer. It's far enough off that I'd mostly put it out of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing much. Carry on working, carry on saving. Maybe I'd think about buying a small flat, since rent's dead money and I'd have time to pay some off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but it's a decade. I've got more pressing things, like my knee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said old buildings are messy. Do you think that buys you time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. A robot can wire a new office, fine, but a 1930s shop with three owners' worth of bodges? I've found cables in old shops held up with a bootlace. Machines will have a hard time with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything for you about family or settling down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it'd push me to buy somewhere sooner, so I'm not paying rent when the work dries up. I'm single, so it's just me deciding. That's easier and harder at the same time.

say: I'd say **ten years** is too far ahead for anyone to know.
At the depot half of us would **laugh it off**, and I'd stay quiet online.
think: I'd be **40** in 2039 and probably still doing **call-outs** until then.
**Old buildings** are messy, which might buy me some extra time.
do: Carry on working and **saving** as usual.
Look at buying a **small flat** so rent isn't dead money.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of his mind, with his **knee** more pressing.
S4.quote: I've found cables in old shops held up with a bootlace.
fieldNote: Believes **old buildings** will protect his kind of work longest.
A long warning lets him push it **out of mind**, true to his resistant style.
The scenario nudges him toward **buying a flat**, his one forward step.

steps.text: Keep doing call-outs and saving at the usual rate
Look at buying a small flat to stop paying rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have no plan and no time to make one. What would help is a firm or a college telling me straight what to train for, and paying me while I do it. I'm not going to guess, I'll get it wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the care homes. If a robot's doing the 2 a.m. fire alarm job, who do the night staff talk to? Half the job at a care home at 2 a.m. is calming people down.

headlineQuote: Half the job at a care home at 2 a.m. is calming people down.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old maintenance electrician** doing call-outs to shops, offices and care homes.
He lives alone, rents, and **never uses AI**; he scrolls past the firm's fault suggestions.
He feels calm in **AI Plateau** but **alarmed** by AGI in 2028, with no plan.
He knows waiting costs him, yet needs to **see robots** on real jobs before acting.
He believes **messy old buildings** will protect his work longest.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no plan and no time to make one.
whatWouldHelp: A firm or college telling him **what to train for** and paying him while he does.
